intro.en: Rev 1 — narration from the recording, cleaned ("clax / climax / Klemax / CLMAX" → CLmax, "row" → rho (ρ), "aerrow foil / aeraf foil / aerof foil / aaf foil" → aerofoil, "pre-torm" → pre-stall, "noble tin camber" → no camber, "sidel maneuvers" → sideslip manoeuvres, "crews" → cruise, "platform" → planform, "Nassels" → nacelles, "weight" (behind the body) → wake, "slaps" → slats, "TAZ" → TAS, "MAC" → Mach, "ATA" → ETA (glider), "ainers" → airliners, "1516" → 15/16, "CLCD" → CL/CD; the last word "Hey" is a cut-off). Before teaching: (1) pages 4 and 10 — lower density does NOT reduce lift at the same indicated airspeed. IAS measures dynamic pressure (½ρV²), so at the same IAS, CL and wing area the lift is the same; lower density reduces lift at the same TRUE airspeed, which is why hot/high take-offs need a higher TAS and longer runs. In the equations V is TAS (or use EAS with sea-level density); (2) page 12 — the slide says the minimum-drag point is "the most efficient angle of attack… optimal efficiency for cruise". Wrong: minimum CD is not maximum L/D. Best L/D is where a line from the origin is tangent to the polar (the recording says this correctly); (3) page 15 — the graph and "key observation" say the best-L/D peak moves to higher calibrated airspeed with altitude. In the low-speed theory used here, best L/D occurs at the same angle of attack and the same EAS (≈ IAS/CAS for light aircraft); only TAS rises (∝ 1/√σ). The slide's own "practical takeaway" box says this — teach the takeaway, not the graph; (4) page 14 — "40 % fuel savings potential" for +1 L/D point is wrong (the recording itself disowns it); +1 point at L/D 15 is ≈ 6 % less drag. "15–20" typical range: airliners ≈ 15–20+, light aircraft much lower (C172 ≈ 9:1, SME); (5) page 7 — "fast aerofoil: higher critical angle / slow aerofoil: lower critical angle" is a weak generalisation; for PPL teach that camber and thickness raise CLmax, that adding camber (or flap) lowers the stalling angle slightly, and that thin sections tend to stall abruptly at the leading edge; (6) remove "[cite: …]" tags printed on pages 11, 13, 15 and 16; (7) fleet link: C172S VS0 40 KIAS / VS1 48 KIAS and best glide 68 KIAS at 2,550 lb (POH — confirm, SME); T206H and DA42 figures from the POH/AFM (SME).

pages.on: Title text and lesson overview: lift and drag coefficients, formulas, design and performance; fighter image.
pages.en: Welcome to coefficients in aerodynamics. In this lesson we explain why engineers and pilots use aerodynamic coefficients and how they let us describe lift, drag and pitching moment in a way that stays meaningful across different aircraft sizes and flight conditions. The key idea is that coefficients are dimensionless. Instead of dealing with forces that change dramatically with speed, altitude or wing size, we use coefficients to normalise the problem. That makes aerodynamic behaviour easier to analyse, easier to compare, and easier to apply from one aircraft or one test condition to another. The three most important coefficients we will focus on are the lift coefficient CL, the drag coefficient CD and the moment coefficient CM. You will see how they connect directly to the standard force equations, where lift and drag depend on dynamic pressure and reference area, and how the coefficients change with angle of attack and configuration. We will also use them to interpret real aerodynamic behaviour: how CL increases with angle of attack until it reaches CLmax and why exceeding the critical angle causes a stall; how CD varies with shape and lift, and why the CL–CD polar helps identify efficient operating points; and how the lift-to-drag ratio becomes a practical measure of efficiency in cruise, climb and glide. By the end you should be able to look at coefficient graphs and equations and immediately translate them into performance — what the wing is doing, what the aircraft will feel like, and what that means for efficiency and safety.

pages.t: Why coefficients are used in aerodynamics
pages.on: Infographic: dimensionless values (model vs full scale), generalisation (wind tunnel → full-scale flight), key examples CL, CD, CM with formulas.
pages.en: Aerodynamic coefficients are used because they turn messy, changing real-world forces into clean, comparable numbers. First, coefficients are dimensionless. Lift and drag forces change dramatically with air density, speed and wing size. If you double the speed, the force increases about four times. If you change altitude, density changes. If you change the aircraft size, the reference area changes. A coefficient removes those scaling effects by normalising the force with dynamic pressure and a reference area. That means you can describe the aerodynamic behaviour of a wing in a way that is not tied to one speed or one aircraft size. Second, coefficients enable generalisation. Once a wing or aircraft has a known relationship, such as CL versus angle of attack, you can apply it across many conditions. Wind-tunnel tests, flight tests and simulations become transferable. If two wings have a similar shape and operate in similar flow regimes, their coefficient trends can be compared directly. This is why engineers can use model-scale testing to predict full-scale behaviour, and why performance charts can be built for a range of weights and altitudes. Finally, coefficients give practical performance insight. The lift coefficient CL tells how effectively the wing produces lift for the given dynamic pressure and area; it is central to the stall, because the stall occurs at CLmax. The drag coefficient CD captures how much aerodynamic resistance exists for the same reference conditions and helps identify efficient configurations and speeds. The moment coefficient CM describes the pitching tendency and is essential for stability, trim and control analysis. In short, coefficients let us describe aerodynamics in a universal language that makes analysis, comparison and prediction possible across different aircraft and flight conditions.

pages.on: Infographic: L = CL·½ρV²·S; variables CL, ρ, V, S; applications: aircraft design, flight planning.
pages.en: The lift equation is one of the most useful tools in aerodynamics because it connects what the wing is — its size and shape — with what the air is doing — density and speed. Lift = CL × ½ × ρ × V² × S. It can also be read as lift equals CL times dynamic pressure times wing area, because ½ρV² is the dynamic pressure. What does each variable mean? CL, the lift coefficient, is a dimensionless number that tells how effectively the wing is producing lift in its current condition; it depends mainly on angle of attack, wing shape and configuration, such as flap setting. Rho is air density — how "thick" the air is. Density decreases with higher altitude and higher temperature, which reduces lift for the same true airspeed and configuration. V is airspeed, the speed of the airflow relative to the wing; because it is squared, speed has a very strong effect — a small increase in airspeed produces a large increase in lift. S is the reference wing area; more area means more lift for the same speed, density and CL. How is it used in practice? It lets you calculate or predict lift under changing conditions, which is essential for engineering and operations. In aircraft design: sizing the wing area and selecting the aerofoil and planform so the aircraft meets its stall-speed, take-off, landing and cruise requirements. In performance planning: understanding how hot and high conditions lower density, reduce lift capability, increase take-off distance and lower climb performance. In flight technique: explaining why increasing angle of attack, which raises CL, can compensate for reduced speed — up to the critical angle — and why increasing speed is such an effective way to increase lift. A practical mental model: lift increases when CL increases, when the air is denser, when speed increases or when wing area increases, and the strongest single driver in the equation is V squared.

pages.on: Graph CL vs α (−10° to +10°, through the origin); linear relationship; zero lift at zero angle; helicopter blade and vertical stabiliser examples.
pages.en: For a symmetrical aerofoil, the CL–alpha relationship — lift coefficient versus angle of attack — is one of the clearest examples of textbook aerodynamic behaviour. First, a reminder: a symmetrical aerofoil has identical upper and lower surfaces, so its camber line lies on the chord line. In ideal conditions it produces approximately zero lift at 0° angle of attack and shows a near-linear increase of CL with angle of attack in the normal range. Because its characteristics are balanced for positive and negative angles, it is commonly used where predictable, reversible behaviour matters, such as aerobatic aircraft, helicopter rotor blades and many tail surfaces. We start with the symmetrical aerofoil because it gives the clearest introduction to the CL–alpha graph: it is simple, nearly linear in the normal range, and passes through zero lift at zero angle of attack. Once you understand this baseline, it is much easier to see what changes with other aerofoils, especially cambered sections, because you can compare how their curves shift relative to the symmetrical reference. Linear relationship: over the normal pre-stall operating range the CL–alpha curve is approximately a straight line. If you increase angle of attack by a small amount, the lift coefficient increases by a proportional amount. The slope of this line is called the lift-curve slope. In real life it is not perfectly linear forever, but it is close enough across the working range that pilots and engineers can predict lift changes reliably as angle of attack changes. Zero lift at zero angle: because the upper and lower surfaces are identical, there is no camber. At zero angle of attack the pressure distribution is symmetric as well, so the net lift is approximately zero; on the CL–alpha plot the straight line passes through the origin — CL equals zero when alpha equals zero. Why is this useful? It is valuable whenever you want neutral, reversible behaviour. Helicopter rotor blades: the blade sections see changing angles of attack as they rotate, and symmetrical sections give predictable behaviour around zero lift. Vertical stabilisers and some tail surfaces: they often operate near small angles of attack in normal flight and need a consistent response for stability and control, including in sideslip. The practical takeaway: for symmetrical aerofoils lift increases almost linearly with angle of attack in the normal range, and the aerofoil produces essentially no lift at zero angle of attack — which is why it is favoured where balanced, predictable characteristics are needed.
pages.th: สำหรับ aerofoil แบบสมมาตร ความสัมพันธ์ CL–alpha หรือสัมประสิทธิ์แรงยกกับมุมปะทะ เป็นตัวอย่างพฤติกรรมตามตำราที่ชัดเจนที่สุดอย่างหนึ่ง ทบทวนก่อนว่า aerofoil สมมาตรมีผิวบนและผิวล่างเหมือนกัน เส้น camber จึงทับเส้น chord ในสภาพอุดมคติจะให้แรงยกประมาณศูนย์ที่มุมปะทะ 0° และ CL เพิ่มเกือบเป็นเส้นตรงตามมุมปะทะในช่วงปกติ เพราะคุณลักษณะสมดุลทั้งมุมบวกและมุมลบ จึงใช้กันมากในงานที่ต้องการพฤติกรรมที่คาดเดาได้และกลับทิศได้ เช่นเครื่องบินผาดแผลง ใบพัดเฮลิคอปเตอร์ และพื้นผิวหางหลายแบบ เราเริ่มจาก aerofoil สมมาตรเพราะเป็นบทนำที่ชัดที่สุดของกราฟ CL–alpha คือเรียบง่าย เกือบเป็นเส้นตรงในช่วงปกติ และผ่านแรงยกศูนย์ที่มุมปะทะศูนย์ เมื่อเข้าใจรูปพื้นฐานนี้ ก็จะเห็นได้ง่ายว่าอะไรเปลี่ยนไปเมื่อเป็น aerofoil แบบอื่น โดยเฉพาะแบบมี camber เพราะเทียบได้ว่ากราฟเลื่อนไปจากเส้นอ้างอิงแบบสมมาตรอย่างไร ความสัมพันธ์เชิงเส้น ในช่วงใช้งานปกติก่อน stall กราฟ CL–alpha เกือบเป็นเส้นตรง ถ้าเพิ่มมุมปะทะเล็กน้อย CL จะเพิ่มเป็นสัดส่วนกัน ความชันของเส้นนี้เรียกว่า lift-curve slope ในความจริงไม่ได้เป็นเส้นตรงตลอด แต่ใกล้พอในช่วงใช้งานที่นักบินและวิศวกรทำนายการเปลี่ยนแรงยกตามมุมปะทะได้อย่างน่าเชื่อถือ แรงยกศูนย์ที่มุมศูนย์ เพราะผิวบนและล่างเหมือนกัน จึงไม่มี camber ที่มุมปะทะศูนย์การกระจายความดันก็สมมาตรด้วย แรงยกสุทธิจึงประมาณศูนย์ บนกราฟ CL–alpha เส้นตรงผ่านจุดกำเนิด CL เท่ากับศูนย์เมื่อ alpha เท่ากับศูนย์ มีประโยชน์อย่างไร มีค่ามากเมื่อต้องการพฤติกรรมที่เป็นกลางและกลับทิศได้ ใบพัดเฮลิคอปเตอร์ หน้าตัดใบพัดเจอมุมปะทะที่เปลี่ยนไปขณะหมุน หน้าตัดสมมาตรให้พฤติกรรมที่คาดเดาได้รอบแรงยกศูนย์ แพนหางดิ่งและพื้นผิวหางบางแบบ มักทำงานใกล้มุมปะทะเล็ก ๆ ในการบินปกติ และต้องตอบสนองสม่ำเสมอเพื่อเสถียรภาพและการควบคุม รวมทั้งขณะ sideslip สรุปในทางปฏิบัติ สำหรับ aerofoil สมมาตร แรงยกเพิ่มเกือบเป็นเส้นตรงตามมุมปะทะในช่วงปกติ และแทบไม่มีแรงยกที่มุมปะทะศูนย์ จึงเหมาะกับงานที่ต้องการคุณลักษณะที่สมดุลและคาดเดาได้

pages.on: Graph: positively cambered curve above the origin, negatively cambered curve below; Cessna and aerobatic examples.
pages.en: For cambered aerofoils the CL–alpha graph looks similar in shape to the symmetrical one in the normal pre-stall range, but it is shifted up or down, because camber creates lift even when the angle of attack is zero. With a positively cambered aerofoil the curve starts above the origin: at alpha equals 0° the aerofoil already has a positive CL. Another way to say this is that the aerofoil reaches zero lift at a negative angle of attack — its zero-lift angle is below 0°. This built-in lift is why positively cambered sections are used on most fixed-wing aircraft: they produce the required lift with less angle of attack, improving efficiency in normal upright flight. With a negatively cambered aerofoil the opposite happens. The curve starts below the origin, so at alpha equals 0° the aerofoil produces negative lift, and it reaches zero lift at a positive angle of attack. These aerofoils are uncommon on main wings, but they can be useful where designers want a surface to generate downforce naturally or to provide specific control behaviour, or where performance in inverted or unusual attitudes matters. So the key difference is the vertical shift: positive camber shifts the CL–alpha curve upward and negative camber shifts it downward, changing how much lift exists at zero angle and where the zero-lift angle occurs.
pages.th: สำหรับ aerofoil ที่มี camber กราฟ CL–alpha มีรูปร่างคล้ายแบบสมมาตรในช่วงปกติก่อน stall แต่เลื่อนขึ้นหรือลง เพราะ camber สร้างแรงยกได้แม้มุมปะทะเป็นศูนย์ สำหรับ aerofoil ที่มี camber บวก กราฟเริ่มเหนือจุดกำเนิด ที่ alpha เท่ากับ 0° aerofoil มี CL เป็นบวกอยู่แล้ว พูดอีกแบบคือ aerofoil จะมีแรงยกเป็นศูนย์ที่มุมปะทะติดลบ มุมแรงยกศูนย์ (zero-lift angle) ต่ำกว่า 0° แรงยกที่มีอยู่ในตัวนี้คือเหตุผลที่เครื่องบินปีกตรึงส่วนใหญ่ใช้หน้าตัด camber บวก เพราะได้แรงยกตามต้องการด้วยมุมปะทะที่น้อยกว่า เพิ่มประสิทธิภาพในการบินหัวตั้งปกติ สำหรับ aerofoil ที่มี camber ลบจะกลับกัน กราฟเริ่มใต้จุดกำเนิด ที่ alpha 0° จะให้แรงยกเป็นลบ และมีแรงยกศูนย์ที่มุมปะทะเป็นบวก aerofoil แบบนี้พบน้อยบนปีกหลัก แต่มีประโยชน์เมื่อผู้ออกแบบต้องการพื้นผิวที่สร้างแรงกดลงเอง หรือให้พฤติกรรมการควบคุมเฉพาะ หรือเมื่อสมรรถนะในท่าบินกลับหัวหรือท่าแปลก ๆ มีความสำคัญ ความต่างหลักจึงเป็นการเลื่อนในแนวตั้ง camber บวกเลื่อนกราฟ CL–alpha ขึ้น camber ลบเลื่อนลง เปลี่ยนปริมาณแรงยกที่มุมศูนย์และตำแหน่งของมุมแรงยกศูนย์

pages.on: Fast aerofoil (thin, small camber, lower CLmax, "higher critical angle", fighter) vs slow aerofoil (thick, large camber, higher CLmax, "lower critical angle", bush plane).
pages.en: Aerofoils are often tailored either toward high-speed efficiency or toward low-speed lift capability, and the design choices show up mainly as differences in thickness and camber. A fast aerofoil is usually thinner, with smaller camber. The thin profile reduces profile drag and delays strong compressibility effects as speed increases, which suits high-speed cruise. With less camber it produces less lift for a given angle of attack and usually has a lower maximum lift coefficient, CLmax. The main objective is efficiency at speed: lower drag, smoother pressure recovery and good performance in the cruise regime. A slow aerofoil is typically thicker, with larger camber. More camber increases lift at lower angles of attack and supports a higher CLmax, which is valuable for take-off, landing and low-speed manoeuvring. Thickness also gives more forgiving low-speed behaviour and structural depth for spars and internal components. The trade-off is more drag at higher speeds. In practical terms, designers choose fast sections when the mission demands high cruise speed and efficiency, and slow sections when the mission demands a low stall speed, short-field performance and strong lift at low speed.

pages.on: Three panels: high-lift designs (flap & slat, cargo aircraft), low-drag designs (airliner), specialised profiles (symmetrical for control surfaces/aerobatics; supersonic/transonic).
pages.en: Aerofoil types are chosen to match an aircraft's mission, because every design is a trade between lift capability, drag and handling qualities. High-lift aerofoils use greater camber and often more thickness to produce strong lift at low speeds, giving lower stall speeds and better take-off and landing performance. They are common on aircraft that need short-field capability, such as bush aircraft and some cargo or utility designs, and they often work together with high-lift devices like flaps and slats to push maximum lift even higher. Low-drag aerofoils are typically thinner with less camber, optimised to reduce profile drag and perform efficiently in cruise, especially at higher speeds. They are widely used on high-performance and transport aircraft, where fuel efficiency and speed matter most, because they deliver a strong lift-to-drag ratio in cruise. Specialised profiles are built for specific handling or speed environments. Symmetrical aerofoils are used on control surfaces and aerobatic aircraft because they behave predictably around zero lift and work well at both positive and negative angles of attack. Other specialised sections are designed for transonic and supersonic flight, where compressibility dominates, often with sharper leading edges or shapes tailored to manage shock waves and wave drag. In short, aerofoil choice is about best fit: high lift for low-speed capability, low drag for efficient cruise, and specialised sections for unique control or high-speed requirements.

pages.on: CLmax at the peak of the CL–α curve; stall phenomenon (attached vs separated flow, sudden loss of lift); importance in design; note: stall angle measured relative to the relative wind, not pitch attitude.
pages.en: CLmax is the maximum lift coefficient an aerofoil can produce. It is the peak of the CL–alpha curve and it sets an important limit on the aircraft's low-speed capability. A higher CLmax generally means a lower stall speed and better take-off and landing performance for a given weight and wing area. A stall occurs when the wing exceeds its critical angle of attack and the airflow can no longer stay smoothly attached to the upper surface. The boundary layer separates, lift drops sharply and drag increases significantly. The key point is that the stall is fundamentally an angle-of-attack event, not simply a low-speed event, although stalls are usually met at low speed because a high CL is then needed. This is why CLmax and stall behaviour are central to design and safety. Designers use them to size the wing, select aerofoil sections and choose high-lift devices — flaps and slats — to achieve the required stall margins, runway performance and controllability. Pilots use the same concepts for performance planning and safe speed management in all phases of flight. And the note is critical: the stall angle is measured relative to the relative wind, not the aircraft's pitch attitude. An aircraft can stall with the nose not very high — for example in a steep turn or a pull-up — and it can be nose-high without stalling if the flight path and airflow direction keep the angle of attack below the critical value.
pages.th: CLmax คือสัมประสิทธิ์แรงยกสูงสุดที่ aerofoil สร้างได้ เป็นยอดของกราฟ CL–alpha และเป็นขีดจำกัดสำคัญของความสามารถที่ความเร็วต่ำ CLmax ที่สูงกว่าโดยทั่วไปหมายถึงความเร็ว stall ต่ำกว่า และสมรรถนะการขึ้นลงดีกว่าที่น้ำหนักและพื้นที่ปีกเดียวกัน stall เกิดเมื่อปีกเกินมุมปะทะวิกฤต และการไหลของอากาศไม่สามารถเกาะผิวด้านบนได้อย่างราบเรียบอีก boundary layer แยกตัว แรงยกลดลงฮวบ และแรงต้านเพิ่มขึ้นมาก ประเด็นสำคัญคือ stall เป็นเหตุการณ์ของมุมปะทะโดยพื้นฐาน ไม่ใช่แค่เหตุการณ์ความเร็วต่ำ แม้มักเจอ stall ที่ความเร็วต่ำเพราะตอนนั้นต้องใช้ CL สูง นี่คือเหตุผลที่ CLmax และพฤติกรรม stall เป็นหัวใจของการออกแบบและความปลอดภัย ผู้ออกแบบใช้เพื่อกำหนดขนาดปีก เลือกหน้าตัด aerofoil และเลือกอุปกรณ์เพิ่มแรงยก flap และ slat ให้ได้ระยะเผื่อ stall สมรรถนะทางวิ่ง และการควบคุมตามที่ต้องการ นักบินใช้หลักเดียวกันในการวางแผนสมรรถนะและจัดการความเร็วอย่างปลอดภัยในทุกช่วงการบิน และหมายเหตุนี้สำคัญมาก มุม stall วัดเทียบกับลมสัมพัทธ์ ไม่ใช่ท่าก้มเงยของเครื่อง เครื่องอาจ stall ได้ทั้งที่หัวไม่ได้เชิดมาก เช่นในการเลี้ยวชันหรือการดึงขึ้น และอาจเชิดหัวสูงโดยไม่ stall ถ้าทางบินและทิศการไหลของอากาศทำให้มุมปะทะต่ำกว่าค่าวิกฤต

pages.on: Infographic: D = CD·½ρV²·S; variables CD, ρ, V, S (wing planform or frontal area); applications: design optimisation, performance prediction.
pages.en: The drag equation mirrors the lift equation and lets us estimate aerodynamic resistance under different flight conditions and configurations. Drag = CD × ½ × ρ × V² × S. Here CD is the drag coefficient, a dimensionless measure of how "draggy" the aircraft or surface is in a given configuration; rho is air density; V is airspeed; and S is the reference area — for aircraft performance work usually the wing planform area. The term ½ρV² is the dynamic pressure, which explains why drag rises rapidly as speed increases. In application, the key is that CD changes with configuration and operating condition. The clean configuration usually has a lower CD; extending flaps or landing gear, or deploying spoilers, increases CD. CD also varies with angle of attack, because induced and pressure-related drag change as the lift demand changes. By selecting the right CD for the configuration and combining it with the current density, airspeed and reference area, engineers and pilots can calculate drag to support performance prediction, power- and thrust-required estimates, cruise-efficiency planning, and take-off and landing configuration analysis.

pages.on: Streamlined shapes (low drag, minimal flow separation; train/race car) vs blunt shapes (high drag, large turbulent wake; truck/space capsule). "[cite: 1]", "[cite: 2]" printed in the text.
pages.en: The drag coefficient CD is strongly influenced by shape, because shape determines how well the airflow can stay attached to the surface and how large the wake becomes behind the object. With streamlined shapes, the goal is to guide the airflow so it stays attached as long as possible. A streamlined body has a rounded nose and a gradually tapering tail, which lets the pressure recover smoothly as the air moves toward the rear. When pressure recovery is gentle, the boundary layer can remain attached — the airflow follows the contour instead of breaking away. The result is a smaller wake, less turbulence and a smaller pressure difference between the front and the back of the object. Since a large part of the drag on many bodies is pressure drag, also called form drag, reducing separation directly lowers CD. This is why fuselages, engine nacelles and fairings are carefully shaped with smooth contours and clean transitions: they minimise disturbance and keep CD low, especially in cruise. With blunt shapes, separation occurs much earlier. The flow cannot turn sharply around the body, so it breaks away and forms a wide turbulent wake. That wake is a region of low pressure, while the front of the object remains at relatively high pressure. The larger the front-to-back pressure difference, the greater the pressure drag and the higher the CD. Blunt shapes can also add unsteady turbulence, which adds drag and noise. Even though blunt shapes are aerodynamically inefficient, they are sometimes unavoidable because of structural, payload, cooling or packaging needs. When that happens, designers add fairings, fillets or carefully shaped edges to reduce separation and recover some of the lost efficiency.

pages.on: Three panels: parabolic relationship; minimum drag point (CDmin) labelled "most efficient angle of attack… optimal efficiency for cruise"; performance analysis (climb, cruise, high speed).
pages.en: The CL–CD graph, often called the aerofoil polar or drag polar, plots how an aerofoil's lift coefficient relates to its drag coefficient as angle of attack changes. Axes: the horizontal axis is CD — moving right means more drag; the vertical axis is CL — moving up means more lift. The parabolic curve: as you increase angle of attack from a low value, CL increases, but CD also increases, so the plotted points trace a curve that is often roughly parabolic. A common way to read the shape is that there is a baseline drag at low lift, called CD0 — the profile or parasite-related drag — and as lift increases, additional drag grows rapidly; for a complete aircraft this lift-related part is mainly induced drag. That is why the curve bends further to the right as CL becomes larger. Minimum drag point: near the bottom of the curve is the minimum-CD region, where the aerofoil operates at the angle of attack of lowest drag coefficient. Note that minimum drag is not the same as maximum efficiency. Best efficiency, maximum L/D: efficiency is measured by the lift-to-drag ratio. On the polar, L/D equals CL divided by CD, which is the slope of a straight line drawn from the origin to a point on the curve. The best L/D is where that line from the origin is tangent to the polar. This point is key for performance; for many aircraft it links to best glide and efficient cruise. High-lift, near-stall region: as you move higher on the curve toward CLmax you approach the stall; drag rises quickly because the angle of attack is high and the flow is closer to separation. Past the stall the polar becomes irregular and is not a region for efficient flight. How configuration changes it: flaps, slats, surface roughness or gear generally shift the polar to the right — more CD for a given CL — and often allow a higher achievable CL, changing both the minimum-drag point and the best-L/D point.

pages.t: Lift-to-drag ratio (L/D) — a measure of aerodynamic efficiency
pages.on: Polar with tangent from the origin marking (L/D)max; climb and high-speed points; impact on performance (fuel efficiency, range, endurance); design optimisation; "[cite: 56]" tags.
pages.en: The lift-to-drag ratio, written CL/CD or simply L/D, is one of the clearest measures of aerodynamic efficiency. It tells you how much useful lift you get for the cost of drag. When the ratio is high, the wing or aircraft produces a lot of lift with relatively little drag, so it can fly with less thrust or power. In performance terms a higher L/D means better fuel efficiency, greater range and longer endurance, because the aircraft needs less energy to stay airborne. It also strongly affects glide performance: the maximum L/D corresponds to the best-glide condition, giving the greatest horizontal distance for a given loss of height in still air. Designers pay close attention to L/D because it is not a single fixed number. It changes with angle of attack, configuration — flaps, gear, spoilers — speed and flight regime. They optimise wing shape, aspect ratio, twist, taper and surface smoothness to improve L/D where the aircraft spends most of its time, usually cruise, while still ensuring safe low-speed handling and stall margins. In short, L/D is a practical efficiency score that connects aerodynamic design choices directly to real-world performance.

pages.en: Here is a more accurate way to present these three points, with the reason behind each. First, 15 to 25: typical cruise efficiency of powered aircraft. Many commercial airliners sit roughly in the 15 to 25 L/D range in cruise, while general aviation is lower, about 7 to 15, depending on configuration and mission. Second, 70-plus: high-efficiency sailplanes. Modern high-performance gliders reach very high glide ratios — the ETA is commonly cited at over 70 to 1 — which shows how far aerodynamic efficiency can be pushed when you do not have to compromise for engines, payload and high-speed requirements. Third, fuel savings: what +1 point of L/D usually means. One point is meaningful, but 40 % is not a typical result. In steady cruise, thrust required is essentially drag, and drag is approximately weight divided by L/D. So improving L/D from 15 to 16 reduces the required thrust by the ratio 15/16 ≈ 0.94 — about a 6 % reduction in that simplified comparison. Real-world savings vary with engine efficiency, altitude, speed schedule and operational constraints. As a rule of thumb, about 1 % less drag gives about 1 % less fuel burn in cruise-focused improvements.

pages.t: How L/D relates to altitude: two different answers
pages.on: Left: max L/D the same at any altitude. Centre graph: L/D vs KCAS at 0, 15,000 and 30,000 ft — peaks at higher KCAS with altitude ("Peak L/D ≈ 15.5 at ≈ 180 KCAS"). Right: airspeed required changes; practical takeaway "same AoA and about the same IAS; TAS increases ∝ 1/√ρ"; real-world exceptions (Mach).
pages.en: The big message of this slide is that altitude does not really change how efficient the wing can be, but it does change the speed at which you achieve that efficiency. Start on the left panel, which answers the first question: does the best L/D change with altitude? For the same aircraft in the same configuration — clean wing, same flap setting — and ignoring compressibility and Reynolds-number effects, the maximum L/D is essentially the same at any altitude. That is because L/D is the ratio of CL to CD, and those coefficients depend mainly on angle of attack, not directly on air density. In the centre graph there are three curves, for sea level, 15,000 ft and 30,000 ft. The peak height of the curves is about the same, meaning the best L/D value is similar at each altitude. Note: the graph shows the peaks moving to the right on a calibrated-airspeed axis; in the theory used here the peak stays at the same EAS (≈ CAS at low speed) and only the true airspeed moves to the right. The right panel explains why: as density decreases with altitude, you must fly faster through the air — a higher true airspeed — to achieve the same lift coefficient. The practical takeaway is that best L/D happens at about the same angle of attack and about the same indicated airspeed for a given weight, but the TAS increases with altitude. Finally, the note at the bottom reminds you that in real high-altitude flight Mach number and compressibility can raise drag, so the ideal picture bends as you approach high-speed buffet limits.

pages.t: How L/D relates to airspeed: the efficiency curve
pages.on: L/D vs airspeed: very slow (high CL, high induced drag), moderate (max L/D, best glide), very high (parasite dominant). Practical implications: best glide; if weight increases (higher best-L/D IAS, max L/D unchanged); if you add drag (gear/flaps lower and shift the curve).
pages.en: If you follow the curve from left to right, it shows a simple idea: L/D changes with airspeed because the mix of induced drag and parasite drag changes with airspeed. Start on the left, the very slow speed region. The curve is low here because at low speed the aircraft must fly at a high lift coefficient to support its weight, and a high lift coefficient means a lot of induced drag. You are paying a big drag penalty just to keep enough lift, so the lift-to-drag ratio is poor. Move toward the middle, the moderate speed region. Here the curve rises to the peak, marked maximum L/D. At this speed the lift coefficient is in an efficient range: induced drag has come down compared with slow flight, but parasite drag has not risen too much yet. This point is the best overall compromise between the two drag types — that is why it is labelled best efficiency and best glide; it is where you get the most lift for the least drag. Now look to the right, the very high speed region. Even though the lift coefficient is low here, the curve drops again because parasite drag dominates: as you go faster, skin-friction and form drag rise strongly, so total drag increases and efficiency decreases. Finally, the bottom row shows the practical consequences. The best-glide speed corresponds to the peak. If weight increases, you need a higher airspeed to reach the same efficient lift coefficient, so the best-L/D speed shifts higher, while the maximum L/D value stays about the same. If you add drag with gear or flaps, the whole curve drops and the best point shifts, meaning maximum L/D is lower and occurs at a different speed.
